raw_text:
Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is an idiopathic systolic heart failure syndrome presenting toward the end of pregnancy or in the months after delivery, classically with left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) <45% and no alternative cause of cardiomyopathy [1], [2]. Although uncommon, it is a leading cause of maternal cardiovascular morbidity and death, and its heterogeneous course—ranging from complete recovery to transplant or death—makes early recognition essential [3], [4], [5].

Incidence varies markedly by ancestry, geography, ascertainment, and obstetric risk profile. Contemporary US administrative studies report rising diagnoses, partly reflecting older maternal age, hypertensive disorders, multifetal gestation, and improved recognition [6], [7], [8]. Black ancestry is consistently associated with higher incidence and worse recovery, suggesting interacting genetic, vascular, and social determinants [9]. PPCM may present before delivery or postpartum; earlier presentation is often associated with more severe disease and fewer antecedent hypertensive disorders [10]. Global registry data confirm major regional differences in presentation, treatment access, and outcomes [30].

The pathobiology is multifactorial. A central model links late-pregnancy oxidative stress to cleavage of prolactin into an antiangiogenic, proapoptotic 16-kDa fragment, producing endothelial injury and cardiomyocyte dysfunction [11]. Complementary work implicates antiangiogenic imbalance, particularly soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1, which may explain overlap with pre-eclampsia and twin pregnancy [12]. PPCM also overlaps genetically with dilated cardiomyopathy: familial clustering, truncating variants in TTN, and other cardiomyopathy genes identify a subgroup with intrinsic myocardial susceptibility [13], [14], [15], [16]. Thus, PPCM is best viewed not as a single disease but as pregnancy-triggered heart failure arising from vascular, hormonal, inflammatory, and genetic vulnerability.

Diagnosis requires a high index of suspicion because dyspnea, edema, fatigue, and orthopnea overlap with normal pregnancy. Red flags include resting tachycardia, hypoxemia, pulmonary edema, elevated natriuretic peptides, cardiomegaly, new murmur, syncope, or thromboembolism. Echocardiography is the cornerstone, documenting reduced LVEF, chamber size, right ventricular function, valvular regurgitation, pulmonary pressures, and intracardiac thrombus. Cardiac magnetic resonance can help exclude myocarditis, infarction, or infiltrative disease when clinically feasible, but absence of late gadolinium enhancement does not exclude PPCM. Coronary, valvular, congenital, tachycardia-mediated, hypertensive, toxic, and pre-existing genetic cardiomyopathies should be considered.

Prognosis is driven mainly by baseline LVEF, left ventricular size, right ventricular dysfunction, race, and timeliness of guideline-directed therapy. In the IPAC cohort, most recovery occurred within 6 months, but women with LVEF <30% or marked dilation had substantially lower recovery and higher event rates [17]. US clinical series similarly show that delayed diagnosis and severe systolic dysfunction predict persistent cardiomyopathy [18], [19]. Contemporary European cohorts demonstrate improved survival with structured heart-failure care, but a meaningful minority still progress to chronic heart failure [20]. African cohorts have reported later presentation, more advanced disease, and higher mortality, emphasizing the importance of access to diagnostics, anticoagulation, and advanced heart-failure therapy [21].

Management follows standard heart-failure principles adapted to pregnancy and lactation. During pregnancy, loop diuretics, beta-blockers, hydralazine–nitrate therapy, and digoxin may be used when indicated, while angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, angiotensin receptor–neprilysin inhibitors, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, and sodium–glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors are avoided until after delivery. Postpartum, full guideline-directed medical therapy should be instituted and titrated. Bromocriptine, which suppresses prolactin, improved LVEF in a small randomized pilot study and showed favorable recovery in a larger randomized trial comparing short and longer regimens, but it requires concomitant anticoagulation and remains variably adopted [22], [23]. Biomarker studies support the biologic relevance of antiangiogenic pathways, but biomarkers have not replaced clinical risk stratification [24]. Delivery timing should be individualized by maternal and fetal status; vaginal delivery is generally preferred unless obstetric or hemodynamic indications favor cesarean delivery [25]. Because PPCM carries risk of ventricular arrhythmia yet may recover, wearable defibrillators can bridge the early high-risk period and help avoid premature implantable cardioverter-defibrillator placement [26].

Counseling about future pregnancy is essential. Subsequent pregnancy after PPCM carries recurrent heart failure risk, especially if LVEF has not normalized, and persistent LV dysfunction is generally considered a strong contraindication [27]. Even after apparent recovery, relapse can occur; shared decision-making should include preconception echocardiography, medication review, genetic counseling when appropriate, and close surveillance through pregnancy and postpartum [28]. Hypertensive disorders identify a partially overlapping phenotype with better average recovery in some cohorts, but they do not eliminate recurrence risk [29]. Overall, PPCM illustrates how pregnancy can unmask cardiovascular vulnerability; progress will depend on equitable early diagnosis, mechanistically informed therapy, and long-term cardio-obstetric follow-up.
